title: Audit log custody and reindex runbook
content:
Purpose:
This runbook describes the custody model, retention tiers, and operational procedures for our audit log storage and indexing pipeline, with concrete steps for common backfill and failure scenarios. It ties audit-event lifecycle (ingest -> index -> archive -> export) to RBAC and evidence automation requirements so Security and SRE teams can reliably reconstruct, export, and prove chain-of-custody for regulatory and incident investigations.

Scope:
- Applies to structured audit events generated by Redwood services (API auth, model inference requests, console changes, private deployment actions).
- Covers primary indexing in OpenSearch, cold archival in GCS (Parquet), and SIEM export (batch to Splunk/forwarder or streaming Kafka).
- Excludes raw application logs and metrics (handled by log-warehouse runbooks).

Retention tiers and custody model:
- Hot (0-30 days): OpenSearch indices with daily rollover (index name: audit-YYYY.MM.DD). Fast query SLA for live investigations.
- Warm (31-90 days): Read-optimized OpenSearch indices on warm nodes; ILM: shrink + forcemerge to reduce storage.
- Cold (91-730 days / up to 2 years): Snapshot to GCS in compressed Parquet partitioned by event_date and org_id, store object-level metadata for retrieval.
- Archive (>2 years): Legal hold-only objects retained in cold storage bucket with restricted RBAC and audit of access.
- Deletion: Deletions must pass Compliance/Legal sign-off. Deletion requests produce an immutable deletion ticket ID logged in audit-custody index.

SLOs and SLAs (examples):
- Indexing latency: 99th percentile < 4s for typical event size ( <2KB ) in hosted regions.
- Export to SIEM: daily batches complete within 2 hours of UTC 02:00; streaming exports lag < 1 min under normal load.
- Backfill completion (standard day-range up to 7 days): complete within 24h; larger historical backfills estimated per plan.

Indexing strategy and schema stability:
- Primary keys: event_id (UUIDv4), org_id, event_timestamp, source_service, actor_id, outcome, prev_event_id (optional).
- Use typed mappings with explicit fields for trace_id, request_id, and schema_version. Schema versioning must be included on every event to allow multiple mapping versions to coexist.
- Index name pattern: audit-YYYY.MM.DD-v{schema_version} for clarity during migration.
- Sharding: daily indices default to 3 shards, adjust based on ingest volume for the org. Avoid hot-warm shard reallocation stress during rollovers.
- Deduplication: ingest layer enforces idempotency by event_id + source_service. Downstream reindex jobs also dedupe by event_id.

Pipeline architecture (high-level):
- Producers -> ingestion API (fronted by edge services) -> transform layer (normalize, enrich with org metadata, validate schema) -> write-ahead queue (Kafka) -> indexer workers (bulk to OpenSearch) -> archive writer (batch snapshots to GCS).
- SIEM export: dedicated export job reads validated stream or index snapshot for batch exports; streaming export uses Kafka Connect to Splunk/Kafka clusters.

Backfill and reindex procedures:
- Trigger criteria: detected missing date ranges (monitoring gap), schema migration, corruption, or customer request for rehydration.
- Pre-checks: verify source data availability (raw event topic or object storage), compute budget estimate (GBs, docs), notify downstream teams and affected customers if >24h.
- Strategy options:
  - Reindex-from-index: use OpenSearch _reindex API when source index is intact and only mapping changes are needed. Preferred for <7 day ranges.
  - Reindex-from-raw: rebuild from raw events in Kafka/backup storage for larger or corrupted index ranges. Use our backfill pipeline (backfill-runner) which reads raw topics, normalizes events, and writes to a staging index then promotes.
  - Parquet-restore: when only archive objects exist, run parquet-parsing job (Spark/Dataflow) to transform into bulk-index payloads.
- Checkpointing: backfill-runner writes progress markers to control topic (backfill-progress-{job_id}). Use these to resumable retry.
- Idempotency: all bulk writes include event_id-based upsert semantics. Avoid blind deletes; prefer tombstones written as events.
- Verification: row counts, checksums (CRC32 on canonical JSON), top-k sample diffs, and SLI comparisons to expected distribution (per-org event distribution).

Common failure modes and mitigation (operational):
- Ingest backlog (Kafka lag spike): alert at lag > 15m for primary topics. Mitigation: scale indexer workers, apply temporary rate-limits at edge, or divert low-priority traffic to dedicated queues.
- Partial indexing due to mapping mismatch: detect by mapping_conflict errors in indexer logs. Mitigation: pause backfill, snapshot current indices, roll mapping change to staging, reindex staging then swap aliases.
- Corrupt archived objects (parquet checksum mismatch): mark object as suspect, attempt object rewrite from earlier snapshot, escalate to SRE and Legal if reconstruction fails.
- Duplicate events after retry storms: rely on event_id dedupe and idempotent bulk writes; for indices without dedupe, run dedupe job using event_id as unique key.
- SIEM export rate-limited or dropped: fall back to daily batch snapshot export. Maintain 'export-delivery' queue with retry policy and DLQ.

Operational runbook (step-by-step for a reindex-from-raw):
1) Triage: tagged alert contains range/date and symptom. Confirm that raw topic contains messages for the date range.
2) Communication: create JIRA backfill ticket and post to #sec-ops with ETA and potential customer impact.
3) Snapshot: take OpenSearch snapshot of affected indices (if present).
4) Launch backfill-runner with job_id=<jira>-<timestamp>, supply start/end timestamps and org filters.
5) Monitor backfill-progress topic and backfill-runner logs. Watch for mapping errors and bulk rejection rates.
6) On completion, run verification scripts: counts, CRC checks, sample diffs.
7) Promote staging index to production alias after verification and remove temporary indices.
8) Close JIRA with postmortem notes and update evidence automation ticket to reflect custody chain.

RBAC, evidence automation, and chain-of-custody integration:
- Access controls: GCS archival buckets and OpenSearch write APIs are gated by service accounts. RBAC v2 roles: audit-reader, audit-writer, audit-archiver, audit-admin. Requests to export evidence must be recorded as events in audit-custody index.
- Evidence automation flow: when an evidence request is created (ticket id), an evidence-export job collates events, signs a manifest (SHA256), stores artifacts in a short-lived evidence bucket and writes a custody-record event. All access to evidence artifacts requires audit-windows and ephemeral credentials.

Testing, drills, and validation:
- Quarterly reindex drills on a non-prod org: run a simulated 90-day backfill to validate costs and timings.
- Schema evolution tests: run canary pipeline that processes a mirror of production traffic with new schema changes and validates field-level migrations.
- SIEM export smoke tests: hourly end-to-end checks to Splunk ingest index to ensure connectivity.

Cost and capacity notes:
- Estimate: average daily audit events ~ 25M/day, average event size 1.2KB -> ~33GB/day raw. Plan index sizing with 25% growth buffer.
- Use ILM warm/cold phases aggressively to bound storage costs; prefer columnar compressed Parquet for >90 day retention.

Open action items / unresolved questions:
- Finalize legal retention windows per region (EU vs US) and implement per-org retention policies in ILM.
- Add automated evidence expiration workflow for >2 year archived artifacts subject to legal review.
- Build a small CLI tool for quick event extraction by ticket id (temporary access flow).

Appendix (quick troubleshooting cheats):
- If reindex job fails early with "mapper_parsing_exception": check schema_version on incoming events and adjust staging mapping to include missing fields as keywords.
- To accelerate large backfills, split by org_id shards and run parallel backfill-runner instances.
- When OpenSearch bulk rejections hit 429: reduce batch size and throttle concurrency, then retry with exponential backoff.
